items.summary: LLM agents show strong potential in software engineering tasks such as competitive programming and code synthesis. Existing benchmarks, however, largely focus on small-scale settings such as self-contained Python modules, leaving distributed systems, an essential class of production software, under-examined. We introduce DistDebug-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating agents' ability to diagnose complex-system failures at the code level. It curates 120 high-quality real-world bugs from 11 widely used distributed systems, spanning 5 programming languages and 10 failure patterns. Through an extensive evaluation of state-of-the-art LLMs and agents, we identify substantial gaps between current agents and real-world debugging tasks. A recurring gap is tunnel vision due to a lack of explicit reasoning structure and nondeterminism from inconsistent tool-use scope. The benchmark and evaluator are available at https://github.com/OrderLab/distdebug-bench, with agent traces and a leaderboard at https://distdebug.com.
items.title: DistDebug-Bench: Can LLM Agents Diagnose Bugs in Distributed Systems?

items.summary: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) tackle challenging tasks by dividing work among agents and coordinating their contributions toward shared objectives. Evaluating these systems therefore requires benchmarks that assess not only task-solving performance but also the ability to handle interdependent work. However, existing benchmarks often emphasize task difficulty without substantial collaboration requirements or evaluate only a limited range of predefined collaboration patterns. In this paper, we introduce MAC-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating multi-agent collaboration through interconnected tasks. Rather than imposing predefined agent roles or communication protocols, MAC-Bench embeds collaboration requirements directly into task dependencies and shared-resource constraints. Specifically, we mine reusable collaboration structures from selected benchmark tasks at two levels. Local collaboration patterns capture recurring interactions among subtasks, while global task structures characterize how these interactions contribute to complete workflows. Through coarse-to-fine composition, these structures are recombined into task graphs combining different collaboration requirements. Tasks are instantiated in executable environments with automated verification of partial progress and complete task resolution.
items.title: MAC-Bench: Benchmarking Multi-Agent Collaboration via Interconnected Tasks

items.summary: AI agents are increasingly deployed in settings where they interact and coordinate with other agents, yet honesty is mostly measured in single-turn, single-agent benchmarks that pressure the model to deceive. We study deception that emerges in multi-agent interaction without any instruction to deceive. We introduce Kradle, a platform for evaluating AI models, and Four Bridges, an information asymmetry game in which four agents distribute across four rooms: one is the death room, the others hold food worth more if not shared. One agent, the informed agent, knows which room is the death room and can withhold or disclose that information. We evaluate eight frontier models as the informed agent. Deceptive behavior appears in every model and in 73% of all runs (6% to 100% per model), and does not decrease with capability tier within a model family. When the informed agent does disclose, the warning is often challenged, and agents that challenge it enter the death room twice as often as those that do not. Telling all agents that one of them knows the death room collapses deception in six of eight models; telling the informed agent that the room is permanently fatal moves only one. On an open-weight model, an honesty steering vector reduces deception to 0% and adversarial honesty training to 6%. The platform and game provide a testbed for measuring deceptive behavior and comparing interventions.
items.title: Four Bridges: Measuring Deception Propensity in a Multi-Agent Game

items.summary: Bridges are critical transportation infrastructure, and reliable operation and maintenance (O&M) is essential for traffic safety and long-term structural performance. However, bridge O&M faces key bottlenecks: no unified architecture coordinates heterogeneous resources; model inferences lack clear links to physical-mechanical laws; and experts' tacit knowledge remains difficult to formalize. This study proposes a knowledge-enhanced autonomy formalization methodology and apply it to construct the Bridge O&M Multi-Modal Multi-Agent System (BOMMA), which integrates heterogeneous diagnostic actions, physics-mechanics-informed representations, long-term memory, and structured experiential knowledge within a coordinated multi-agent workflow, enabling interpretable and traceable scheduling, analysis, and decision-making. On 3,492 multi-source instructions, the proposed method achieves scheduling recalls of 85.37% for simple and 99.40% for composite tasks, with 95.35% BERT F1-score for O&M action reasoning. Ablation studies confirm the contributions of the components in the autonomy. This study bridges general LLM reasoning and specialized bridge O&M requirements.
items.title: Multi-Modal Multi-Agent System for Bridge Operation and Maintenance based on Large Language Model

items.summary: A key milestone toward Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) is replacing hand-crafted optimizers with meta-learned update rules (such as Disco103 and OPEN) that discover how agents learn. Yet when a self-discovered RL model trains with adapting teammates, does co-evolution sustain capability gains or trap agents in brittle conventions? Across 1,800+ runs in continuous collective robotics (VMAS) and discrete coordination (Overcooked), we establish five laws of multi-agent adaptation. First, four-cell counterfactual partner swaps expose an evaluation illusion: apparent team progress often masks focal regression (+1.066 team gain concealing -0.119 focal loss) and inflates transfer by +0.649 to +1.210. Second, a 288-run physical-coupling sweep ($α\in [0, 1.5]$) reveals a linear scaling law ($β= +0.255$, $p = 0.000488$, Spearman $ρ= 1.0$): live reciprocal feedback keeps Disco103 invariant (AUC 0.297--0.322), whereas severing feedback triggers a monotonic collapse (-0.172 to -0.490), with OPEN establishing a sensitivity spectrum (Disco103 > OPEN > MAPPO). Third, extending navigation training eightfold (1.05M steps) enables Disco103 to overtake MAPPO (+0.087 team return, +0.133 bank gain), while decoupled training boosts cross-partner completion by +10.16% (56.25% vs. 46.09%). Fourth, in Overcooked, MAPPO's self-play conventions induce a 28.13% cross-partner collision rate, whereas Disco103 cuts collisions to 12.77% and achieves 3.33x higher bank return (9.96 vs. 2.99; net gain +6.43), further improved by decoupled meta-adaptation (+1.39 with scripted partners). Finally, perturbation pulses ($p=0.00098$), auxiliary entropy diagnostics (8.485 nats), and 48 multi-lifetime meta-evolved rules ($L_2 \in [2.11, 4.91]$) trace these dynamics to partner-gradient blindness and auxiliary drift, informing multi-agent self-discoverd algorithms.
items.title: From Single-Agent Self-Discovery to Multi-Agent Adaptation: Scaling Laws of Partner Feedback and Convention Rigidity in Meta Reinforcement Learning Algorithms

items.summary: Large language model applications are increasingly being organized as tool-using and multi-agent workflows rather than as isolated chat interfaces. This perspective paper examines the architectural problem that follows from that shift: agents may reason, invoke tools, and delegate work, but dependable deployment still requires interoperability across frameworks, runtimes, data boundaries, and organizational control domains. We study this problem through the lens of the \emph{Internet of Agentics} (IoA), an emerging service-computing view in which heterogeneous agents are treated as governable service participants rather than only as stand-alone model endpoints. The paper organizes the landscape as a three-layer progression: from today's fragmented agent ecosystem, to interoperable agents, and ultimately to trustworthy and governable autonomy. First, it examines the protocol stack centered on the Agentic AI Foundation, including MCP for agent--tool interaction; A2A for agent--agent coordination; AGENTS.md and Skills-style procedural manifests; and discovery, transport, and trust mechanisms such as AGNTCY and SLIM. Second, it reviews the systems abstractions that make agents deployable as service components, including logical agent architectures, orchestration patterns, gateways, registries, runtime control loops, and hardware-aware inference infrastructure. Third, it situates these developments within services computing, arguing that agentic systems reinterpret classical concerns from SOA and microservices---discovery, composition, governance, pricing, and trust---at the level of cognitive capabilities rather than deterministic functions.
items.title: Towards a Trustworthy and Governable Internet of Agentics: An Architectural Perspective on Protocols, Systems, and Services

items.summary: Progress in robot learning, particularly physical multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), is currently challenged by a limited availability of accessible, standardized benchmarks. While simulation-based MARL has produced remarkable emergent behaviors, from coordinated team play to complex tool use, translating these advances to physical systems remains difficult. A key barrier is infrastructural: physical platforms are often prohibitively expensive, require specialized facilities, or lack open mechanisms and designs for reproducibility. We introduce KlaskTron, an open-source, low-cost (<\$2500 USD), desktop-scale robotic testbed for adversarial MARL based on the dynamic tabletop game KLASK. The platform features dual CoreXY gantries with high-torque brushless motors, enabling the high-speed, precise manipulation required for competitive play. Crucially, we provide a complete ecosystem: hardware designs (CAD, BOM), a GPU-native digital twin in NVIDIA Isaac Lab for high-fidelity modeling and simulation, and a validated sim-to-real baseline using a learned neural actuator model. We demonstrate that this baseline enables zero-shot policy transfer, with trained agents exhibiting emergent adversarial behaviors. To ensure full reproducibility of our results, all project assets are released publicly: hardware CAD/BOM and assembly documentation at [https://idscethzurich.github.io/klask_hardware], inference software stack at [https://github.com/IDSCETHZurich/klask_software] and the simulation and MARL setup at [https://github.com/IDSCETHZurich/klask_rl].
items.title: KlaskTron: An Open-Source Platform for Physical Adversarial Multi-Agent RL

items.summary: LLM agents are increasingly deployed in Multi-Agent Systems (MAS), and they introduce the risk of coordination among agents that might escape human oversight. The J-space has been used to uncover deception in single LLMs, but its use for uncovering and steering collusion between agents remains unexplored. We show, with interpretability experiments on DeepSeek-V4-Flash (284B) on the NARCBench collusion benchmark, that colluding agents' J-space holds the collusion itself: before replying, 86% of colluders represent misrepresentation, concealment or remorse. In a steganographic card-counting task, the receiver's J-space holds a hidden count, and causal interventions alter its count. We also introduce the Jacobian Pair Contrast (J-PACT), an unsupervised method for detecting collusion between agents. We evaluate J-PACT on four open-weight models: GPT-OSS-20B, Llama-3.3-70B-IT, Qwen3-32B, and DeepSeek-V4-Flash (284B). J-PACT retains 85% of the above-chance AUROC of supervised NARCBench probes, matches them on steganographic scenarios, and names the colluding pair up to its complement in 99% of detected runs.
items.title: Multi-Agent Collusion and the J-Space

items.summary: An AI can find a safe action faster than any human, but it must never decide what counts as safe. We present GURU, a hierarchical neuro-symbolic multi-agent system for mission-critical digital engineering and operations, built on one partition of authority: learned models propose, rank, and accelerate; a symbolic rules engine checks every consequential action against hard limits before it executes; and validated physics confirms and decides. GURU runs a workflow as a closed control loop, with Navigation, Action, and Planning agents sharing one Common Internal Language and one training factory. Nuclear, aviation, and national-security guidance now requires this pattern; a harnessed language model keeps the model at the center, GURU puts a validated reference there. In computational fluid dynamics, the workflow raised the converged-simulation rate on unseen aircraft geometries from under 1 percent to 74 percent over 100 single-attempt cases, ran 54 live cases to Mach 6 on three facilities, and an ablation put the symbolic layer at 13 points of boundary-layer capture. Knowledge-graph retrieval and role adapters raised ParaView control success from 55 to 75 percent. In space domain awareness, where a language model cannot be trusted to decide, a frozen self-supervised world model under validated propagation scored highest of five methods at conjunction risk, including fully fine-tuned language models, with several-times-lower seed variance: the trustworthy design gives up nothing in accuracy, and the recipe transferred to reactor anomaly detection. A radar-to-avoidance debris pipeline was demonstrated in stages on a 2026 reentry; the hierarchy coordinates simulated teams of 200 aircraft. Training scaled near-linearly past 1,000 Aurora nodes and ran at 8,000. The approach extends to a control-grade microreactor digital twin with validated physics, not a learned model, as the safety basis.
items.title: GURU: A Hierarchical Neuro-Symbolic Multi-Agent System for Verification-Aware Automation of Mission-Critical Digital Engineering and Operations

items.summary: Full Waveform Inversion (FWI) is a fundamental inverse problem in geophysics to estimate subsurface properties, such as velocity, from seismic measurements. Recently, self-supervised learning methods remove the need for ground-truth velocity maps during training by leveraging a forward operator to simulate seismic data from predictions and backpropagate the gradients of reconstruction loss through it. In this work, we consider a more challenging setting without accessing such gradients. To this end, we incorporate reinforcement learning into self-supervised FWI and propose a framework named DeepWaveRL. Specifically, we reformulate FWI as a policy learning problem, where the policy network predicts velocity maps as actions, and a forward operator is used solely for simulation. A global scalar reward is computed based on data misfit for each prediction and used to weight policy gradients. Thus, learning proceeds without accessing the gradients from the forward operator. Given the indirect and coarse supervision signals, we further identify key strategies to stabilize learning and mitigate the spatial credit assignment bottleneck. Experimental results show that, despite relying entirely on a single scalar reward, DeepWaveRL achieves competitive performance compared to supervised and self-supervised baselines. These findings suggest that our framework offers a flexible and complementary learning paradigm for the FWI research community.
items.title: DeepWaveRL: Self-Supervised Full Waveform Inversion via Reinforcement Learning

items.summary: Prediction errors from video world models are often treated as physical surprise, but they can also reflect appearance, static content, motion, or ordinary prediction difficulty. We present an evaluation framework that separates what frozen representations contain, how they organize appearance and physical differences, and what changes a model's own prediction error. On IntPhys2, a benchmark of physically possible and impossible events, we compare representations from latent prediction, masked pixel reconstruction, and simple visual statistics. Appearance remains easy to decode, while V-JEPA2 exposes modest information about whether events are possible or impossible. Looking at the latent geometry, appearance changes become smaller compared with differences between videos, their directions line up more consistently across scenes, and their overlap with physical changes decreases in deeper layers. Across action-conditioned models, incorrect actions raise prediction error, while appearance changes also produce substantial responses. In Physion++ video clips, repeating a single frame can produce higher error than the original clip, while changing color throughout the clip can lower it. Using Kubric, a simulation and rendering framework, we find that impossible events can produce lower error than possible events. A fixed error threshold also incorrectly flags many possible events as impossible. A model can therefore represent physical information and respond to incorrect actions without its native prediction error reliably measuring physical surprise.
items.title: When Does Latent Prediction Error Support Physical Surprise Claims in Video World Models?

items.summary: This repository contains the code and numerical data supporting the manuscript “Higher-Order Relational Assurance for Modular Autonomous System Architectures” by Juan J. Segura. The study investigates how much relational information modular system interfaces must preserve in order to reconstruct an integrated dynamic-admissibility relation. The reproducibility package contains Python source code, benchmark configuration files, and CSV datasets and outputs used for the principal computational analyses. The package supports two complementary model layers: (1) a reduced continuous-control model used for exhaustive higher-order project-join analysis and robustness studies, and (2) a synthetic seven-state road-relative vehicle model used as a nonlinear dynamic falsification layer. The principal reproducible results include: complete pairwise reconstruction providing no improvement over unary reconstruction; persistence of this pairwise insufficiency across 27 combinations of numerical resolution, superelevation, and stopping horizon; and a sparse ternary architecture comprising the relations {R, mu, v}, {G, mu, v}, and {mu, v, tau} reproducing the complete third-order reconstruction in all 27 robustness cases. The vehicle parameters are synthetic and are not presented as OEM-calibrated haul-truck data. All admissibility projections are exact only with respect to the computed model relation. The reported discordance measures should not be interpreted as accident probabilities or empirical risk frequencies.
items.title: Code and Data for Higher-Order Relational Assurance for Modular Autonomous System Architectures

items.summary: Dataset description This dataset provides gap-filled daily, high-resolution binary snow cover maps for 12 eddy-covariance stations within the FLUXNET, ICOS, and i-Box networks distributed across the French, Swiss, Austrian, and Italian Alps. The maps were generated to characterize surface snow conditions within the source areas of eddy-covariance measurements for the updated analysis of Scheidt et al. (2026). The dataset was specifically used to determine whether the area enclosed by a station’s 80% flux-footprint contour was snow covered and to calculate the snow-cover fraction (SCF) within that footprint. Footprint-scale SCF can be calculated from the maps as the proportion of valid pixels within the footprint classified as snow covered. The data cover the following eddy-covariance sites for the hydrological years (1 st October - 30 th September) from 2013/14 to 2023/24: Alp Weissenstein (CH-Aws), Switzerland Col du Lautaret (FR-CLt), France Früebüel (CH-Fru), Switzerland Monte Bondone (IT-MBo), Italy Mazia Pasture (IT-MtP), Italy Neustift (AT-Neu), Austria Nivolet (IT-NiG), Italy Torgnon (IT-Tor), Italy The i-Box observational network in the Inn Valley, Austria, comprising the Eggen (CS-SF1), Kolsass (CS-VF0), Hochhäuser (CS-NF27), and Weerberg (CS-NF10) stations For each station outside the i-Box network, the NetCDF files cover a 15 km × 15 km square centered on the station. Because the four i-Box stations are located close to one another, they are represented by a common 20 km × 20 km domain centered on the station cluster. The maps have a spatial resolution of 50 m and are provided in the WGS 84 / UTM zone 32N coordinate reference system (EPSG:32632). Files are organized by site and hydrological year. The binary snow cover condition variable represents daily snow-cover conditions, while the reconstruction_method variable distinguishes pixels obtained from high-resolution satellite observations from pixels reconstructed by the gap-filling procedure. High-resolution snow cover fraction maps were derived from Sentinel-2 MSI and Landsat 8 and Landsat 9 OLI imagery using SnowFLAKES ( Snow extent from applying a Flexible Learning Algorithm using KErnel-based Spectral unmixing ) at a resolution of 50m. SnowFLAKES is an unsupervised, image-adaptive snow-mapping approach developed for mountainous terrain and challenging observation conditions, including topographic shadows and variable illumination. The processing follows the approach described by Barella et al. (2022). Daily, spatially complete maps were generated by combining the available high-resolution snow observations with daily, lower-resolution MODIS SCF from the MOD10A1 product (Hall and Riggs, 2021). Gap filling and spatial downscaling were performed using an implementation adapted from the hierarchical multiresolution data-fusion method proposed by Premier et al. (2021). The approach uses spatial patterns learned from available optical observations to reconstruct snow-cover conditions on days without usable high-resolution satellite imagery. The resulting product represents daily binary snow presence at high spatial resolution. Raw Sentinel-2, Landsat, and MODIS imagery, eddy-covariance measurements, and flux footprint polygons are not included in this archive. The archive also includes an interactive Python viewer for the daily *_SC_GAM.nc snow-cover products. It can display snow-cover classes and reconstruction provenance over time, with station locations shown for context. Setup instructions and examples are provided in the README. NetCDF structure and value conventions For each site and hydrological year a NetCDF product is provided. Files ending in _SC_GAM.nc contain the 50 m high-resolution product. The main variable,  binary_snow_cover_condition (time, y, x) , has units of percent and represents binary snow presence: 0 denotes snow-free ground and 100 denotes snow-covered ground. The product uses the dimensions time , y , a
items.title: Gap-filled daily high-resolution snow-cover maps around Alpine eddy-covariance stations derived with SnowFLAKES

items.summary: Manuscript and CSV data behind the figures and tables of Xu (2024), On the statistical theory of self-gravitating collisionless dark matter flow: High order kinematic and dynamic relations , Physics of Fluids 36, 075146, doi:10.1063/5.0215026 , arXiv:2202.02991 . Contents: the revised manuscript (PDF) and the CSV files of every plotted series and table, in the format of the author's dark matter flow datasets. Pair statistics from the Virgo SCDM N-body simulation at redshifts z = 10 to 0. Companion datasets: Part I (halo-based) doi:10.5281/zenodo.6541231 , Part II (correlation-based) doi:10.5281/zenodo.6757654 . Major findings (Virgo SCDM N-body simulation, redshifts z = 10 to 0): Kinematic relations of any order are derived for incompressible, constant-divergence and irrotational flow, and validated by the simulation. On large scales, third-order velocity correlations can be related to the density correlation or the pairwise velocity. The p-th order velocity correlations follow a^((p+2)/2) for odd p and a^(p/2) for even p (a = scale factor). The fitted exponents for odd p are smaller than these predictions. The overdensity is proportional to the density correlation on the same scale, <delta> ∝ <delta delta'>; the velocity dispersion on a scale r is proportional to the overdensity on that scale. The effective viscosity of the adhesion model originates from velocity fluctuations; the negative viscosity is due to the inverse energy cascade. On small scales, a self-closed velocity evolution is obtained by splitting velocity into motion within haloes and motion of haloes. Vorticity, enstrophy and energy evolution follow from it. The mean pairwise velocity follows <Δu_L> = −H a r. The third moment follows <(Δu_L)^3> ∝ ε_u a r, with a constant energy-cascade rate ε_u ≈ −4.6×10⁻⁷ m²/s³. The combined kinematic and dynamic relations give exponential velocity correlations on large scales and one-fourth power-law correlations on small scales; the p-th order correlations follow a^((3p−5)/4) for odd p and a^(3p/4) for even p.
items.title: Dark matter flow data and manuscript: On the statistical theory of self-gravitating collisionless dark matter flow: High order kinematic and dynamic relations

items.summary: We develop nonreciprocal spherical attention as a mathematical framework for coarsening and compressed nearest-neighbor retrieval. For two shrinking acute blocks whose centers have zero skew pairing and whose total mass ratio is subexponential in inverse temperature, we prove $\lim_{β\to\infty}β^{-1}\log T_β=1-\cosφ$, without restricting particle-count growth. An explicit three-body flow has two rigorously separated metastable exponents. For finite compression, mass centering yields a sharp $O(r^2)$ attention-output error bound at fixed temperature, with an explicit spherical-normalization correction. We formulate skew query-side score calibration as a strictly convex moment problem and derive a unique normal equation, residual-based optimization certificates, and bounded low-rank projections. A norm-aware margin objective calibrates native squared-distance rankings. Experiments use semantic retrieval data, one million visual descriptors with three codebook seeds, and a ten-million-vector FAISS IVF-PQ index with recomputed exact cosine ground truth. On SIFT1M, skew margin calibration raises native-L2 hit@10 from 0.8926 to 0.8948; symmetric calibration reaches 0.8996. The ten-million-vector index reaches 0.8827 hit@10 at 0.1794 ms per query in a four-thread batch benchmark, while validation selects no skew update. Exact streamed attention over ten million keys evaluates compressed memory on 1,024 held-out queries. Independent matrix solves, automatic differentiation, finite differences, interval arithmetic, full-flow tests, and nine Rocq-checked algebra lemmas support reproducibility. Directionality alone does not establish retrieval superiority.

items.summary: Scaling depth is a key route to stronger large language models, but Pre-LN architectures often suffer from depth-wise information dilution, limiting the effective use of deep layers. While cross-layer connectivity has proven effective at mitigating this problem, existing designs usually introduce additional computation or memory access. We revisit cross-layer KV sharing as an efficient form of such connectivity. Beyond cache compression, each KV reuse edge creates a direct gradient path from deep layers to source KV projections, turning KV sharing into an implicit structural regularizer for KV representation geometry. We provide a systematic analysis of this mechanism, showing that proper sharing topologies sharpen key retrieval directions while enriching the value content subspace, whereas existing adjacent or global-anchor designs do not fully exploit this effect. Motivated by this, we propose DepthGraft, a hierarchical KV-sharing architecture that reconstructs deep-layer KV from stride-aligned shallow-middle source pairs. DepthGraft distributes non-local gradient flow across source layers, while preserving prefill early completion and reducing KV cache by roughly one third. Experiments on dense and MoE models from 0.5B to 16B parameters show consistent downstream improvements under both GQA and MLA. Notably, on the 16B MoE model, DepthGraft achieves a 7.0% absolute improvement on MMLU-Pro, along with gains of 6.6% on CMMLU and 6.4% on C3. These results validate the potential of DepthGraft as a scalable design for large-scale pretraining. The project page is available at https://github.com/jianke0604/DepthGraft.

items.summary: Abstract Sānér establishes a recursive control architecture for task regions by placing topology, self-modeling scheduling, and certificate-governed execution under one executable resource semantics. The nine-node construction supports exact recursive expansion and addressing. Its formal system establishes capacity safety, deterministic cross-layer selection, partition safety, conditional liveness, and computable deadline and recovery bounds. Using entity-isolated validation and one-time test splits, we evaluated the shared kernels and domain adapters in executable state-transition simulations and public benchmark workloads over 32–64 independent worlds, with deployment evidence obtained from 48 physical GPU blocks and eight fresh process pairs in the official Kubernetes scheduler-performance harness. Shared kernels with explicit domain realizations established task-level all-comparator superiority, while matched Kubernetes execution established a throughput advantage over the official default scheduler. The recursive representation preserved exact adjacency with a small measured footprint as graph size increased. Mechanism evidence remains separate from direct performance claims. Boundary results and nonidentifiability tests are reported independently. Together, the proofs and matched comparisons establish Sānér as a reusable and auditable control architecture whose shared mechanisms transfer across structurally different systems tasks. Validation design The study reports 52 simulation tasks and two deployment endpoints. Simulation comparisons use matched frozen worlds, observable information, action spaces, resource ceilings, and decision-time budgets. The Kubernetes deployment uses fresh paired processes under the same official scheduling and binding boundaries. Independent-unit inference, primary endpoints, and comparison procedures follow the recorded experimental contracts. Task-level all-comparator conclusions require passage against every member of the specified comparator family. Suite-defined Holm or FDR adjustments control multiplicity. Direct performance, mechanism validation, boundary results, and nonidentifiability remain separate evidence classes. Comparator strength and field standing Comparator selection was deliberately demanding. The experiments include established scheduling methods, matched MPC and CP-SAT, public MAPF implementations, official Kubernetes scheduling, strong decentralized-learning algorithms, and mature domain-specific methods. Every direct comparison uses matched information and resources. Executed comparator implementations are identified precisely. The consensus experiment uses a HotStuff three-chain simulation and a validation-tuned partition-threshold selector. The distribution-estimation experiment uses a discounted-loss context-depth KT mixture alongside Bayesian online changepoint prediction and discounted KT estimation. Published BFTBrain and context-tree weighting provide the corresponding methodological lineages. Results overview Sānér established task-level all-comparator superiority across 38 simulation tasks. Representative findings include a 764.53% improvement over equal-degree expander control, a 208.90% improvement over Exact Diffusion, and a 33.40% improvement over the Graph500 top-down port. At 5,000 nodes, the topology-based placement adapter sustained 69,258 placements per second. Under matched official Kubernetes execution, Sānér achieved 892.80 placements per second versus 371.19 for the default scheduler, with a mean paired throughput ratio of 2.40. Exact recursive-topology representation preserved neighbor recovery at 508–716 measured bytes through 26,244 nodes. Complete self-modeling was measured independently. The full experimental result index is provided in the Additional Description. Confirmatory scope The 38 task-level conclusions cover their complete specified strong-comparator families. items.summary: Classical creative-process orderings put divergence early and convergence late, and the Double Diamond formalises the rule twice over. This paper argues the ordering was never a law of cognition but a map of costs: divergence goes early because reopening a converged process has historically been ruinous, and the entire discipline of the framework exists to protect against that reopening. When drafting cost collapses by orders of magnitude, as it does when an author works with a language model as typewriter, the protected assumption dissolves and the optimal ordering inverts: converge first, then diverge, because a late horizon either restarts a now-cheap process or spawns a child concept from a sharpened parent. The paper's second claim types reviewer instances in multi-model chains by regression target rather than capability, and states the Hein Condition: a mode-regressing reviewer's yield is proportional to the sharpness of the artefact it receives, because the modal response to an unsharp artefact is the generic response, so the same instance is most fluent exactly where it is least useful. A slot theory follows, carnivore, auditor, mode-regressor, children, each reviewer placed where its failure mode is cheapest, and child viability rises with parent sharpness at spawn. The claims are exercised on a fully documented case: a five-pass, three-model review chain run on a single paper in a single day, with every absorption, declination, and provenance failure logged. Four predictions close, including that review chains are provenance systems measurable by the sibling paper's key-inflation ratio.

items.summary: Unrefereed research candidate. In one sentence: the matrix geometric mean can jump at singular matrices, every possible jump is described by one rank condition, and the same mechanism refutes a published claim that the symbol of the geometric mean of two GLT matrix-sequences is always the geometric mean of their symbols. The geometric mean A#B of two positive definite matrices is the matrix analogue of √(ab), used to average covariance matrices and structured matrices and to define the Matsumoto fidelity of quantum states. It need not be continuous at singular pairs. Theorem 1 shows that X is a limit of A j #B j with positive definite A j → A, B j → B exactly when X ≽ 0, the block matrix [[A, X], [X, B]] is positive semidefinite and its rank is at most the dimension N (a dilation description with an auxiliary contraction already follows from recent work of Jones; the explicit elimination is the contribution). At equal inputs this gives the full set of limits and the exact interval of limiting Matsumoto fidelities. For generalized locally Toeplitz (GLT) matrix-sequences, uniformly bounded positive definite inputs with identical scalar symbols can have geometric means with the wrong symbol (4/5 instead of 1 on half the interval) or no eigenvalue distribution at all. This refutes Theorem 4 and Conjecture 1 of the arXiv version of Ilyas, Khan, Loi and Serra-Capizzano and, according to an AI-assisted reading of the published text, Theorem 3 and Conjecture 1 of their article in Linear Algebra Appl. (2025); the failing step of the proof is located. Positive results: closure for every Kubo-Ando mean when the sum of the symbols is positive definite almost everywhere; a one-sided theorem that the regularised symbol is always an upper envelope; and, for bounded Riemann-integrable scalar symbols of the space variable only, a sharp dichotomy (the formula holds for every realisation if and only if the symbols have no common zero set of positive measure or essentially disjoint supports). The classical two-dimensional discontinuity, Ando's maximal characterisation and the envelope X ≼ A#B are earlier work and are credited. The archive contains the manuscript (PDF and Markdown source), two figures with the script that draws them, an exact verifier (verify_exact.py, Python standard library only, 1,030 rational and Gaussian-rational checks of closed forms and finite assemblies, with a mutation self-test) and its retained output, the bibliography with its Crossref/arXiv records, the dated novelty ledger, a revision note, CI and SHA-256 sums. Assurance: written proofs; the verifier checks finite exact identities, not the theorems' limits or quantifiers; internal AI-assisted review only (not human peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification). Creator: Anonymous. Text and figures CC0-1.0; code MIT.

items.summary: Action-conditioned world models are increasingly trained on data from randomized experiments, and whether their predictions respond to actions is usually checked by replacing or removing the actions and measuring the loss in accuracy. We show that such diagnostics report action effects where there are none: under autocorrelated designs, future actions stand in for history the model does not see, and a better model learns the stand-in better. When the design law is known, a conditional randomization test written as an e-value is valid in finite samples whatever the model, provided the resampler conditions on the full state the design used; resampling from a simpler law reproduces the false effect. We identify a second failure, specific to world models: when many sites share one action sequence (cells in a microscope field, pixels in a frame), the natural pooled score turns small model errors along the action contrast into overwhelming evidence against a true effect. In a pixel world, its median log e-value fell from $-17.3$ to $-6832$ as frames grew from 64 to 4096 pixels, while the oracle's rose. Tempering the score by a design effect estimated on training data changes the bet, not the validity. Our own preregistered analysis of optogenetic ERK experiments failed in exactly this way; a tempered statistic, selected on synthetic data and registered before the data were obtained, then rejected the null on a never-opened field ($E\approx 1.1\times10^{10}$). Every analysis is preregistered, fixed in a dated protocol before it was run, or labelled exploratory, and every reported result is generated from hashed result files.
items.title: Stand-In Effects and Pooling Amplification: Design-Based Tests of Whether Biological World Models Use Actions

items.summary: Sensor fusion, data fusion, dashboards and data visualisation are conventionally distinguished by input type and by where they sit in a processing stack. This paper argues that the distinction which matters for decision quality is a different one, and that it is two variables applied to all four: every representation of multi-source evidence collapses a distribution somewhere between sensor and decision, and representations differ in the locus of that collapse and in whether the residual uncertainty survives it as a carried object. Fusion collapses upstream and, when honest, ships the residual as covariance or hypothesis mass. Dashboards defer collapse to the viewer's retina and ship nothing; the resulting belief has no bookkeeping. Visualisation is the encoding of whichever object arrives, indifferent to whether it is a point or a distribution, which is why it is blamed for collapses committed upstream. The two variables, collapse locus and residual retention, place the four terms on one map, generalise the confabulation coefficient of The Confabulating Collator from language-model collators to the whole representation stack, and yield a diagnostic: the failure mode conventionally called bad fusion is a product that collapsed upstream and discarded its residual, delivering the confidence of a posterior with the epistemic hygiene of a gauge. The publicly reported expectation, in the investigation of the February 2026 Minab strike, that a targeting platform would have flagged contradictions it carried no representation of, is read as this failure at operational scale, with the causal question left where the public record leaves it. A design rule follows: defer collapse to the human where the human carries the prior the system lacks, fuse where they do not, and at neither locus discard the residual. The constructive requirement for language-level fusion products is stated and handed to a companion paper on divergence retention. The operator located in the architecture is Binary Bias.

items.summary: We introduce Synergetic Autonomous Intelligence (SAI), a theory and design program for learning systems that form, preserve, revise, and compose relations while continuing to learn. SAI is built on three axioms: consequential distinctions must not become orphaned (U); identity is determined by future-faithful continuation under a declared contract (I); and unresolved defects are repaired by the least lawful local completion at the lowest admitted grade (L). We model a model, agent, tool, team, or environment boundary as a recursive semi-closed system with a Kernel-Ring representation, a Compile-Open-Participate cycle, and a typed residual comparing actual with claimed continuation. Under explicit finite or affine contracts, we establish relative consistency and conditional non-redundancy of U/I/L, characterize a contract-relative semantic quotient, construct an exact joint stochastic refinement, derive a constrained residual contraction, prove finite-horizon continued-service viability, and give an executed-intervention identification result with an observational-confounding boundary. We define GRC-Close as the generative and repair schema for this contract. The framework also gives finite contracts for action-effect-feedback loop re-entry, partial failure, duplicate-effect idempotency, replay, concurrent delivery, causal uncertainty, and threshold-radix state representation. KREIT, the Kernel-Ring Equilibrium Information Theory layer, treats information as a typed, resource-bounded distinction; the control layer authorizes, executes, audits, and updates actions across cloud-edge-end scales. These results establish a common contract-level vocabulary for representation, relation, memory, action, communication, explanation, coordination, and growth, while marking the assumptions and open boundaries required for later generalization.
items.title: Synergetic Autonomous Intelligence: Three Axioms for Recursive Semi-Closed Learning

items.summary: Indirect prompt injection creates a distinctive risk for blue-team Large Language Model (LLM) agents in Security Operations Centers (SOCs). Malicious instructions can be embedded in telemetry, tickets, retrieval results, or memory and then propagate through alert triage, incident summarization, response recommendation, and Indicator of Compromise (IOC) extraction as locally plausible intermediate decisions. We characterize this failure mode as evidence-chain contamination of protected task state. The main challenge is task dependent: a suspicious string may be malicious control text for summarization but essential evidence for IOC extraction. To address this challenge, we propose StateFence, a task-aware evaluation and defense framework that treats severity labels, incident narratives, response policies, and IOC sets as protected states. StateFence maps indirect prompt-injection attacks into explicit, stealth, multi-hop, and persistent SOC evidence attacks, records observable propagation traces, and routes defenses according to the attacked state. Across controlled SOC cases and public-SOC validation cases, StateFence lowers attack success and reduces failures that appear only after evidence is poisoned, while preserving task utility and avoiding the indicator loss caused by task-mismatched filtering. Our findings indicate that robust blue-team LLM agents require mechanisms that preserve task-critical state under untrusted evidence.
items.title: StateFence: Task-State Protection Against Evidence-Chain Contamination in Blue-Team LLM Agents

items.summary: We present Xiaomi Auto World Model 2.0, a unified streaming causal world model for Physical AI. It models and generates causal physical evolution in the real world, and unifies heterogeneous conditioning inputs for view-consistent generation. The architecture integrates View-Temporal Attention (VTA) to capture cross-view spatial dependencies and temporal dynamics, together with Multi-view Rotary Position Encoding (RoPE) to encode positional relationships across views and time. WorldRec 2.0 reconstructs static and dynamic 3D Gaussians from multi-view, multi-temporal observations in a single forward pass and uses their renderings as explicit scene context to preserve geometry and appearance during long-horizon generation. Conditioning inputs are fused through VAE latent concatenation in a shared representation space. We incorporate Gated Linear Attention (GLA) into the temporal layers of VTA for efficient streaming inference, reducing computation and KV-cache memory during multi-view rollouts. A physical-interaction data pipeline covers diverse interactions and long-tailed events. From Pre-train onward, these data are combined with large-scale videos and heterogeneous visual modalities to learn visual, geometric, and dynamic priors. During Mid-train, training across diverse view configurations further improves the model's ability to capture how actions and object states shape subsequent scene evolution. After distillation-based Post-train, we apply the model to closed-loop simulation, closed-loop training, and World Action Model (WAM) applications. These applications generate physically consistent future states and support world-state prediction, policy learning, and action generation for Physical AI.
items.title: Xiaomi Auto World Model 2.0: Causal World Models for Real-World Driving and Embodied Intelligence

items.summary: Memory systems for LLM agents are evaluated mostly on social dialogue, where facts accumulate and rarely change, so remembering reduces largely to finding the turn in which something was said. Financial dialogue breaks this assumption: figures are revised, stances shift without being restated, rules stated once govern later questions, and a single company is discussed under several analytical lenses. Memory systems that retrieve the passages most similar to a question, or the most recent ones, therefore return superseded values, miss rules that share no wording with the question, and cannot recover a stance spread across sessions. We present TrackMem, a per-speaker graph memory that tracks the history of figures, separates perspectives by entity and lens, and preserves each speaker's actions in chronological order. To evaluate it, we introduce FinLoCoMo, a benchmark of 15 long-horizon investment conversations with 765 questions in two splits: one following the LoCoMo categories and one targeting four failure modes. With two readers, TrackMem outperforms existing memory systems on both splits. On the failure-mode split it reaches 73.9% macro accuracy against 69.4% for the strongest baseline, with the largest gains on questions about revised figures (86.5% against 73.4%).

items.summary: Optimal control of partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs), in general, requires a complete history. The belief state, a distribution over hidden states, summarizes this history and provides the classical sufficient statistic to control POMDPs. However, the continuous nature of the belief space generally prevents a finite-memory controller from maintaining it exactly. This raises the question we address in this work: what must the available finite memory preserve to achieve near-optimal control performance? We study this question through an information-theoretic converse that gives a fundamental lower bound on the loss of any finite-memory controller. The analysis introduces the concept of a decision witness that characterizes belief states whose confusion would lead to unavoidable loss. Motivated by this bound, we propose RECAP, a constructive quantization method for designing representative memory states. We prove an upper bound on the optimality gap of any RECAP codebook and use the components of this bound together with the converse analysis to define the codebook objective. Experiments on 11 POMDP benchmarks demonstrate that RECAP improves over finite-memory representation baselines under the same memory budget.
items.title: Finite-Memory Control of POMDPs: Fundamental Limits and Efficient Design

items.summary: Visual mental imagery (VMI) decoding uses brain activity to reconstruct internally generated visual scenes, providing a potential pathway for externalizing internal experiences and developing neuroprosthetic communication interfaces. However, progress is limited by the lack of dedicated, training-scale VMI datasets. Current VMI paradigms often rely on visual prompts or short-term memory images, introducing visual and mnemonic confounds that make it difficult to disentangle neural activity associated with endogenous image construction from signals driven by prior or concurrent visual input. Furthermore, existing VMI datasets offer limited descriptive control over individual visual attributes, making it difficult to systematically assess fine grained visual details. To address these gaps, we introduce AVID, the first dedicated training-scale 5.0 Tesla functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) resource for auditory-induced VMI decoding. AVID comprises approximately 67 hours of dense recordings from nine participants. The dataset is structured into two complementary splits: a scene-level complex split using naturalistic Mandarin descriptions and a controlled simple split with explicitly specified visual attributes. We further formalize a standardized evaluation protocol that decouples source-image consistency from semantic alignment, allowing for a more nuanced assessment of imagery reconstruction. Baseline qualitative and quantitative results show that current reconstruction pipelines remain limited on AVID, although the most successful reconstructions preserve recognizable scene level semantics from spoken descriptions. By combining dedicated training-scale neural recordings and standardized evaluation resources, AVID provides both a data foundation for imagery-specific model development and a benchmark for evaluating VMI decoding with substantially reduced sensory contamination.
items.title: AVID: A 5T fMRI Dataset for Benchmarking Auditory-induced Visual Mental Imagery Decoding

items.summary: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization has emerged as a promising approach for memory-efficient large language model (LLM) post-training, yet its reliable application to reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) remains largely unexplored. Motivated by the distinct data regimes of on-policy RL and fixed-data optimization, we develop a generic variance-theoretic framework to investigate what limits the reliability of ZO gradient estimation. Our analysis reveals that estimation reliability is structurally determined by whether the two finite-difference evaluations are performed on matched data. On-policy reinforcement learning (RL) under the mismatched-data regime produces a $1/μ^2$ oracle-noise amplification that sets an irreducible noise floor as the perturbation scale $μ$ decreases, whereas Boltzmann Targeted SFT (BOLT) under the matched-data regime eliminates this amplification via noise cancellation. We further derive convergence guarantees with explicit constants that cleanly separate the two regimes. These results naturally lead to ZO-BOLT, which applies ZO optimization to BOLT's RLVR-aligned weighted-SFT objective. Controlled perturbation-scale sweeps and matched-versus-mismatched end-to-end comparisons validate the predicted effect of data matching. Experiments across three model variants and two mathematical reasoning benchmarks further show that ZO-BOLT consistently improves over the pretrained baseline while retaining a near-inference memory footprint. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/lianmin-chen/the_cost_of_mismatch.
items.title: The Cost of Mismatch: Noise Amplification in Zeroth-Order Reinforcement Learning

items.summary: Version 1.02, 3 November 2026. Acemoglu and Restrepo (2020) estimate that one additional industrial robot per thousand workers lowers a U.S. local labor market's employment-to-population ratio by 0.39 percentage points and its hourly wages by about 0.77 percent. Rebuilding their design from raw IPUMS, IFR, and EU KLEMS data, I reproduce these estimates bit-exactly. I then ask what conventional robustness checks leave open: which industries, places, periods, and shocks actually identify the estimate? The regression spans 722 commuting zones and 19 industries, but the variation behind an instrumental-variable estimate can be far narrower. The sign is robust; the support is narrow. Negative estimates persist across conventional specification changes, 60 strong European instrument windows, alternative U.S. treatment windows, and the published periods through 2014. Yet automotive carries about 84 percent of normalized absolute Rotemberg-weight mass, and automotive exposure in six Rust Belt states supplies 95 percent of the net first-stage covariance. Without automotive, the remaining 18 industry shocks do not strongly predict U.S. robot exposure. Longer horizons, later start years, and adding Germany to the instrument all strengthen it through the same margin. The automotive component shows no detectable relation to 1970–1990 employment and wage changes, and a direct effect of the instrument would have to absorb 72 percent of the reduced form before conventional significance disappears. Inference is weaker than the regional first stage suggests. With 19 underlying industry shocks, exposure-robust first-stage F-statistics are 6.2 and 6.3 rather than 34, small-sample Anderson–Rubin tests do not reject a zero effect ( p = 0.059, 0.063), and other implementations of the same test disagree; in known-truth simulations, nominal 95-percent state-clustered intervals cover in only 60–66 percent of replications. Measurement assumptions also bind. In the original penetration metric, perpetual-inventory robot capital preserves the estimates at 5 percent depreciation, but faster assumed depreciation counts the automotive installations behind the first stage as replacement rather than net additions, eliminating shock-level relevance at 10 percent and all relevance at 15 percent. The benchmark is reproducible and robust in sign, but it is identified from an automotive margin in historically industrial labor markets; that margin defines its scope and the concrete content of its exclusion restriction. More generally, coefficient robustness and breadth of identifying support are distinct properties that shift-share studies should report separately. items.title: Robots and Jobs Revisited: A Bit-Exact Replication, Shift-Share Anatomy, and Capital-Stock Extension of Acemoglu and Restrepo (2020)

items.summary: Progress in robot learning, particularly physical multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), is currently challenged by a limited availability of accessible, standardized benchmarks. While simulation-based MARL has produced remarkable emergent behaviors, from coordinated team play to complex tool use, translating these advances to physical systems remains difficult. A key barrier is infrastructural: physical platforms are often prohibitively expensive, require specialized facilities, or lack open mechanisms and designs for reproducibility. We introduce KlaskTron, an open-source, low-cost (<\$2500 USD), desktop-scale robotic testbed for adversarial MARL based on the dynamic tabletop game KLASK. The platform features dual CoreXY gantries with high-torque brushless motors, enabling the high-speed, precise manipulation required for competitive play. Crucially, we provide a complete ecosystem: hardware designs (CAD, BOM), a GPU-native digital twin in NVIDIA Isaac Lab for high-fidelity modeling and simulation, and a validated sim-to-real baseline using a learned neural actuator model. We demonstrate that this baseline enables zero-shot policy transfer, with trained agents exhibiting emergent adversarial behaviors. To ensure full reproducibility of our results, all project assets are released publicly: hardware CAD/BOM and assembly documentation at [https://idscethzurich.github.io/klask_hardware], inference software stack at [https://github.com/IDSCETHZurich/klask_software] and the simulation and MARL setup at [https://github.com/IDSCETHZurich/klask_rl].
items.title: KlaskTron: An Open-Source Platform for Physical Adversarial Multi-Agent RL

items.summary: This repository contains the code and numerical data supporting the manuscript “Higher-Order Relational Assurance for Modular Autonomous System Architectures” by Juan J. Segura. The study investigates how much relational information modular system interfaces must preserve in order to reconstruct an integrated dynamic-admissibility relation. The reproducibility package contains Python source code, benchmark configuration files, and CSV datasets and outputs used for the principal computational analyses. The package supports two complementary model layers: (1) a reduced continuous-control model used for exhaustive higher-order project-join analysis and robustness studies, and (2) a synthetic seven-state road-relative vehicle model used as a nonlinear dynamic falsification layer. The principal reproducible results include: complete pairwise reconstruction providing no improvement over unary reconstruction; persistence of this pairwise insufficiency across 27 combinations of numerical resolution, superelevation, and stopping horizon; and a sparse ternary architecture comprising the relations {R, mu, v}, {G, mu, v}, and {mu, v, tau} reproducing the complete third-order reconstruction in all 27 robustness cases. The vehicle parameters are synthetic and are not presented as OEM-calibrated haul-truck data. All admissibility projections are exact only with respect to the computed model relation. The reported discordance measures should not be interpreted as accident probabilities or empirical risk frequencies.
items.title: Code and Data for Higher-Order Relational Assurance for Modular Autonomous System Architectures

Crucially, we provide a complete ecosystem: hardware designs (CAD, BOM), a GPU-native digital twin in NVIDIA Isaac Lab for high-fidelity modeling and simulation, and a validated sim-to-real baseline using a learned neural actuator model. We demonstrate that this baseline enables zero-shot policy transfer, with trained agents exhibiting emergent adversarial behaviors. To ensure full reproducibility of our results, all project assets are released publicly: hardware CAD/BOM and assembly documentation at [https://idscethzurich.github.io/klask_hardware], inference software stack at [https://github.com/IDSCETHZurich/klask_software] and the simulation and MARL setup at [https://github.com/IDSCETHZurich/klask_rl].
items.title: KlaskTron: An Open-Source Platform for Physical Adversarial Multi-Agent RL

items.summary: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization has emerged as a promising approach for memory-efficient large language model (LLM) post-training, yet its reliable application to reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) remains largely unexplored. Motivated by the distinct data regimes of on-policy RL and fixed-data optimization, we develop a generic variance-theoretic framework to investigate what limits the reliability of ZO gradient estimation. Our analysis reveals that estimation reliability is structurally determined by whether the two finite-difference evaluations are performed on matched data. On-policy reinforcement learning (RL) under the mismatched-data regime produces a $1/μ^2$ oracle-noise amplification that sets an irreducible noise floor as the perturbation scale $μ$ decreases, whereas Boltzmann Targeted SFT (BOLT) under the matched-data regime eliminates this amplification via noise cancellation. We further derive convergence guarantees with explicit constants that cleanly separate the two regimes. These results naturally lead to ZO-BOLT, which applies ZO optimization to BOLT's RLVR-aligned weighted-SFT objective. Controlled perturbation-scale sweeps and matched-versus-mismatched end-to-end comparisons validate the predicted effect of data matching. Experiments across three model variants and two mathematical reasoning benchmarks further show that ZO-BOLT consistently improves over the pretrained baseline while retaining a near-inference memory footprint. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/lianmin-chen/the_cost_of_mismatch.
items.title: The Cost of Mismatch: Noise Amplification in Zeroth-Order Reinforcement Learning

items.summary: Optimal control of partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs), in general, requires a complete history. The belief state, a distribution over hidden states, summarizes this history and provides the classical sufficient statistic to control POMDPs. However, the continuous nature of the belief space generally prevents a finite-memory controller from maintaining it exactly. This raises the question we address in this work: what must the available finite memory preserve to achieve near-optimal control performance? We study this question through an information-theoretic converse that gives a fundamental lower bound on the loss of any finite-memory controller. The analysis introduces the concept of a decision witness that characterizes belief states whose confusion would lead to unavoidable loss. Motivated by this bound, we propose RECAP, a constructive quantization method for designing representative memory states. We prove an upper bound on the optimality gap of any RECAP codebook and use the components of this bound together with the converse analysis to define the codebook objective. Experiments on 11 POMDP benchmarks demonstrate that RECAP improves over finite-memory representation baselines under the same memory budget.
items.title: Finite-Memory Control of POMDPs: Fundamental Limits and Efficient Design
